body:
what does this achieve over the annotation roles already performed by using semantic HTML elements and ARIA attributes?

https://ogp.me feels related as well

Microdata formats exist already - for example [schema.org](https://schema.org/docs/gs.html) - which can be used to provide rich data structures for scrapers and indexers. They can leverage the `item*` attributes (.e.g. `itemprop`, `itemid`, `itemtype` etc) attributes as they see fit. These attributes can include multiple URLs so can be used to describe parts of a page using multiple formats including but not limited to schema.org. If you find schema.org insufficient, I'd encourage you to reach out to that group - or perhaps build an alternative that leverages those attributes.

If you want to create your own standard that differs from the existing `item*`, or `aria-*` namespaces, the HTML standard isn't the correct venue to discuss or progress this, I believe. External specifications can create their own defacto attribute namespaces without any requirements from the HTML standard (much like `aria-*` does).

Given you have already put the work in to specify a namespace with `aid-*` - the repository you link to - I am not sure there's anything actionable here for the HTML specification.

Keith's answer is a good summary of why this is not suitable for the HTML Standard.

I will also add my personal opinion that proposals like this are misguided. We have a long history of trying to make the web more semantic by trying to get web developers or tools to create more informative markup. The goal is then to make it easier for machines to consume the web.

Although these have had some small successes, in a large part they have not proved useful. Instead, what's worked is for companies to work on making the machines that consume the web smarter, to the extent that they can consume the 99% of the web that is authored with humans in mind instead of machines.

(This goes back to the earliest days of the web, when people thought `<meta name="keywords">` was the right way to encode keywords. In fact, what worked better was improving search engine crawlers so they could extract keywords automatically for their indices.)

Especially these days, it seems unwise to bet against that trend, and try to design a vocabulary that is directed at AI tools. Instead, I'd bet on AI tools continuing to get better at being able to interface with the human-oriented web, with no special markup affordances or effort required from web developers.
